newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ruehe says optimism on NATO-Russia deal growing.
newsitem.headline: Ruehe says optimism on NATO-Russia deal growing.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Tuesday he was more optimistic than ever before that NATO and Russia would reach an agreement on a deal to allow the alliance to expand into eastern Europe.
Speaking to a group of German and U.S. business leaders in Stuttgart, Ruehe said Russia was in the process of constructively examining a number of NATO suggestions on its proposed enlargement.
"The chances of reaching an agreement on a joint document that will extend far into the future were never as favourable as right now," Ruehe said, according to a text of his remarks released in Bonn.
"Even if the negotiations are difficult, I am confident that an agreement will be signed this summer."
Russia remains firmly opposed to NATO's plans to offer membership to several former Warsaw Pact countries this summer, saying they represent a threat to its own security.
Ruehe, who due was to meet U.S. Secretary of Defence William Cohen in Bonn later on Tuesday, said it was necessary for Russia to move forward from its old way of thinking.
"What is now needed is a new rhetoric from Moscow, one that departs from thinking about spheres of influence and balance of power and accepts the new NATO for what it is," Ruehe said.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, the man charged by the alliance with negotiating a new, all-embracing post-Cold War deal with Moscow, will return to Moscow at the weekend for more talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
The two men will for the first time have drafts of a possible future agreement on a NATO-Russia Council, a new forum allowing permanent and across-the-board consultations on security issues.
Moscow wants any documents between the two to be legally binding and to contain commitments that NATO's military infrastructure will not be moved eastwards.

NATO favours a more flexible approach. It says the new deal, endorsed by alliance heads of state, will be politically binding, but a treaty would be unwieldy and take months to pass through national legislatures.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic lead the field of a dozen countries clamouring to join the most powerful military alliance ever assembled with Slovenia and Romania making late last-minute pushes for inclusion in the first round.
